texts.full_text: the molecular mechanisms through which mGluR5 activation induces hypersensitivity are unclear. In addition, mGluR5 is expressed throughout the nervous system, but the specific role of mGluR5 expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons (nociceptors) is unknown. I will address both of these issues through the experiments in this proposa l. The proposed research plan has four specific aims: 1. To assess the expression and function of mGluR5 in mouse models of chronic inflammatory pain; 2. To test the hypothesis that mGluR5 expressed on nociceptors plays a critical role in inflammation-induced hypersensitivity; 3. To identify the molecular pathways through which mGluR5 activation induces peripheral sensitization; and 4. To assess whether mGluR5 expression is regulated by injury or inflammatory mediators. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that mGluR5 expressed on nociceptors plays a critical role in the development and maintenance of chronic pain states. The rationale for these experiments is to determine if peripheral mGluR5 activation contributes to hypersensitivity, as well as identify downstream pathways through which mGluR5 regulates pain. The proposed research will provide insight into mechanisms that underlie inflammatory pain. It also may lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets for treatment of pain. This project addresses a critical gap in our understanding of how chronic inflammation causes persistent hypersensitivity. This work is important because it could help us better understand why many people have chronic pain and how we can develop new treatments to help these individuals. The javascript engine is probably casting to a string because the string type is suitable for names of object properties. Try this more traditional approach: stuff = []; stuff[0] = 3; for(var i=0; i<stuff.length; i++) { var x = stuff[i]; alert(typeof x); } A: for..in To clarify, the behavior you're observing is due to how JavaScript handles enumeration with `for...in` loops and array indexes. When using a `for...in` loop on an object or array in JavaScript, it iterates over all enumerable properties of that object (including inherited ones), treating property names as strings because they are essentially keys in the underlying key-value pairs structure of objects/arrays. Here's why this happens: 1. Enumeration: `for...in` is designed to enumerate through an array or object’s properties, including indexes which it treats as string identifiers (keys). This behavior ensures compatibility with property names that can be any valid identifier name in JavaScript. 2. Property Keys are Strings: In JavaScript arrays and objects, keys/property names are always strings under the hood to maintain consistency across different types of properties you might encounter—whether they’re numeric indexes or string-based identifiers like `"firstName"` on an object. 3. Inherited Properties: While not directly relevant here since arrays don't typically have inherited enumerable properties, it's worth noting that `for...in` can also enumerate over these if present in the prototype chain of objects you’re iterating through.
